What the orchard taught us in its first year

When our neighborhood group planted the community orchard last spring, most of us knew next to nothing about fruit trees. We knew we wanted apples and pears, we knew the old lot behind the library was sitting empty, and we knew that a few dozen people were willing to give up their Saturday mornings. That was about the extent of our plan. A year later, we have forty-two trees in the ground, thirty-eight of them still alive, and a much better idea of what we are doing. I want to write down what we learned, partly for our own records and partly for any other group thinking about trying the same thing.

The first lesson was about soil. We assumed that the lot, which had been a lawn for decades, would be fine for trees. It was not. When we finally had the soil tested in early summer, after several of the young trees had started to look yellow and tired, the results showed heavy clay, poor drainage, and very little organic matter. We should have tested before we planted, and anyone starting a project like ours should do that first. A basic test costs very little through the county extension office, and the people there will help you analyze the results and decide what to add.

We spent most of June working compost into the ground around each tree, which was hard and slow work in the heat. The volunteers who showed up for those mornings deserve a lot of credit. By the end of July, most of the trees had recovered, and a few had put on surprising growth. We lost four, all in the lowest corner of the lot, where water collected after every storm. We have since dug a shallow drainage channel there, and we plan to replant that corner next spring with trees that tolerate wet feet better.

The second lesson was about people. At our first meeting, more than sixty people signed up to help. By midsummer, the regular crew was down to about fifteen. That is normal, I am told, and it does not mean the others lost interest. It means that people have busy lives and that a project like this needs a small, steady core rather than a large, occasional crowd. We found that the best way to keep people involved was to give each of them a specific tree, or a specific job, that was theirs. When a volunteer knew that a particular pear tree was their responsibility, they came back to check on it, even on weeks when there was no work day scheduled.

We also learned to keep the work days short. Our early sessions ran for four or five hours, and people drifted away before the end. Once we cut them to two hours, with a clear list of tasks posted at the start, attendance went up and more got done. It turns out that people are happy to give two focused hours, and much less happy to give a whole morning of standing around while someone figures out what to do next.

The third lesson was about pests. We had read about aphids and codling moths, and we were ready for them, more or less. We were not ready for the deer. In late August, a small group of deer discovered the orchard and stripped the lower branches of nearly every tree in a single night. We put up a temporary fence the following weekend, which has mostly kept them out, but the damage set several trees back by a season. A proper fence is now the top item in our budget for next year. If you are planting anywhere near open land, plan for deer from the start.

The aphids, when they came, were easier to handle than we expected. A few volunteers took on the job of checking the trees every week and spraying the worst spots with water and a mild soap solution. We also planted a border of flowers along the edge of the lot, which seems to have drawn in ladybugs and other helpful insects. By the end of the summer, the aphid problem had more or less taken care of itself.

The fourth lesson was about money. Our first-year budget was small, and most of it came from a single grant from the city. We spent more than we planned on soil amendments and on the fence, and less than we planned on tools, because several members donated their own. Going into the second year, we are trying to build a broader base of support. We held a small fundraiser in the fall, with cider from a nearby farm and a raffle of donated prizes, and it raised enough to cover the new fence. We are also talking with the library about a joint program, since the orchard sits right behind their building and a lot of their visitors walk past it every day.

The fifth lesson, and maybe the most important one, was about patience. Fruit trees take years to produce a real harvest. Some of our younger volunteers were disappointed to learn that we would not be picking apples in the first fall, or even the second. We have tried to keep people engaged by focusing on the small milestones, like the first blossoms, the first new branches, and the first time a tree made it through a storm without damage. We also started a simple logbook, kept in a box at the gate, where anyone can write down what they notice. Reading back through it now, it is a lovely record of a year of slow progress.

Looking ahead, we have a few goals for next year. We want to replant the wet corner, finish the permanent fence, and add a small shed for tools so that volunteers do not have to carry everything back and forth. We also want to start a monthly workshop on pruning and tree care, led by a retired arborist who lives on the next street over and has offered to help. And we want to keep working toward our larger goal, which is an orchard that the whole neighborhood feels is theirs, where anyone can stop by, pick a piece of fruit, and sit for a while under the trees.

I want to end by thanking everyone who helped this year. The orchard exists because people gave their time, their tools, their money, and their patience to a patch of empty ground. It is still a young orchard, and it will be years before it looks the way we imagine it. But it is growing, and so are we. If you have been thinking about joining us, the next work day is the first Saturday of the month, and we would love to see you there. Bring gloves, and maybe a friend.

A short note for other groups. If you are planning a similar project, start small, test your soil, plan for deer, and give your volunteers real ownership. Those four things would have saved us a lot of trouble. Everything else, you can learn as you go, the same way we did. And keep a logbook from the very first day, because the memory of what you tried and what failed fades faster than you would think, and the notes are worth far more in the second year than the effort they cost in the first.
